#4757. Healthgrades Announces Top Hospitals for Specialty Care, Outpatient Procedures

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Hospital ratings have become an important resource for choosing where to receive care. They influence which doctors patients choose, how far they are willing to travel, and whether they seek care at a different facility.

On October 27, Healthgrades announced the recipients of the 2027 Specialty Excellence Outpatient Awards and Specialty State Rankings.

The annual awards recognize hospitals delivering outstanding patient outcomes in specialty care across the United States. Healthgrades is the leading platform used by Americans for finding a doctor or hospital.

New research from Healthgrades highlights that hospital quality is increasingly a factor in healthcare decisions.

Around 80% of patients report that when looking for a doctor, the quality of the hospital where they practice matters. Additionally, 7 in 10 patients (68%) say they’re more likely to seek care for a procedure or health condition from a doctor who works at a hospital with high quality ratings.

What’s more, around 71% of patients say they would switch doctors to gain access to a higher-rated hospital.

“Our specialty awards identify the nation’s top-performing hospitals across numerous medical specialties, helping consumers find high quality care tailored to their specific needs,” said Alana Biggers, MD, MPH, medical advisor at Healthgrades.

Healthgrades is owned by RVO Health. By clicking on this link, we may receive a commission. Learn more.

“Navigating the complex healthcare system can feel daunting, but taking a proactive stance to understand where to access superior care can enhance your healthcare journey and overall experience. The ability to make informed decisions about your health — and where to get care — is a cornerstone of self-advocacy, and we are proud to help make that information accessible to all patients.”

Healthgrades identifies hospitals that deliver exceptional outcomes across common outpatient procedures and specialty conditions.

Finding high quality care is important, particularly amid a growing gap between top-performing and one-star hospitals.

According to Healthgrades, from 2023 to 2025, if all hospitals had performed at the five-star level from 2023 to 2025:

“One of the biggest challenges is balancing increasing patient needs with the resources available to healthcare professionals,” Biggers said.

“Hospitals face workforce shortages, growing administrative responsibilities, financial pressures, and increasing complexity in patient care. Physicians and other healthcare professionals need adequate time and support not only to evaluate and treat patients, but also to communicate results, coordinate follow-up care, and address concerns that arise between visits,” she continued.

“When healthcare teams are adequately supported, they are better positioned to communicate effectively with patients, coordinate care, and address patients’ needs.”

Biggers said that ensuring equal access to quality healthcare is challenging because of factors such as:

Hospital closures and reduced services make access even more difficult. Biggers identified a few possible solutions, such as expanding outpatient care, building community partnerships, using telehealth when appropriate, and improving coordination among healthcare providers.

“Ultimately, providing high quality care requires more than clinical expertise. It requires healthcare systems to invest in their workforce, strengthen care coordination, and create environments where healthcare professionals have the resources they need to provide safe, effective, and patient-centered care,” Biggers said.

“Equally important, healthcare systems must ensure that patients have meaningful access to these services, regardless of where they live or their socioeconomic circumstances.”

Healthgrades acknowledges hospitals that excel in three aspects of specialty care:

Biggers said that outstanding hospitals recognize that high quality care extends beyond just treating an illness.

“It involves listening to patients, understanding their individual circumstances, and ensuring they feel respected, informed, and involved in their healthcare decisions,” she said.

Patients want to find a hospital that excels in the procedures or health conditions relevant to them.

The recipients of the Specialty Excellence Awards are among the top 15% of hospitals specializing in these areas.

Healthgrades evaluated patient outcomes at roughly 4,500 hospitals across 31 common procedures and conditions to reach their decisions.

Among the list of Specialty Excellence Award recipients, Healthgrades also recognizes America’s 100 Best Hospitals for Specialty Care for 11 specialty areas andAmerica’s 50 Best Hospitals for Specialty Care for four specialty areas.

“An outstanding hospital prioritizes both patient care and the people delivering that care,” Biggers told Healthline.

“While clinical outcomes, patient safety, and access to evidence-based treatments are essential measures of quality, I believe hospitals must also invest in workforce development and support. This means ensuring physicians, nurses, and other healthcare professionals have appropriate staffing levels, adequate clinical and administrative support, and opportunities for continued professional development,” she continued.

Healthgrades awards U.S. hospitals that excel at Outpatient Orthopedic Surgery, Outpatient Joint Replacement, andOutpatient Prostate Care.

Outpatient care is one of the fastest-growing areas of healthcare. The number of orthopedic procedures performed in an outpatient environment has grown exponentially in recent years.

From 2020 to 2025, outpatient hip replacement procedures grew by 81%, while inpatient procedures dropped by 75%. Outpatient knee replacements increased by 71% while inpatient volumes decreased by 70%.

“I believe several factors are contributing to the growing demand for outpatient care, including advances in medical technology, a greater emphasis on preventive care, and the increasing need to manage chronic medical conditions,” Biggers said.

“Many services and procedures that previously required hospitalization can now be safely performed in outpatient settings. Patients also appreciate the convenience of receiving care closer to home and avoiding unnecessary hospital stays,” she added.

To meet the increasing demand for outpatient procedures, Biggers cautioned that healthcare systems must ensure that these services are adequately staffed and supported.

“Effective communication and coordination between outpatient providers, specialists, and hospitals are essential to maintaining continuity and quality of care,” she said.

State Rankings identify the top three or five hospitals in eligible states across 19 key specialty areas.

The rankings are based on clinical performance and build on the 2027 Healthgrades Specialty Excellence Awards Methodology.

State-level specialty care rankings help consumers find outstanding local hospitals for their condition or procedure.

The analysis used Medicare inpatient data from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) from 2023 to 2025, and assessed patient outcomes across 31 conditions and procedures.

These outcomes served as the foundation for determining Specialty Excellence Awards and state hospital rankings.

With consumer-facing awards and ratings influencing healthcare decisions, transparency about their methods and limitations remains essential.

Ratings can help patients ask better questions and compare options, but they should complement — not replace — clinical guidance and informed decision making.

#4756. Can a CAPTCHA Make You Think About God?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

You have done it hundreds of times. A grid of blurry squares appears; you click the ones with traffic lights, and you move on. Nobody has ever asked what was going through your mind while you proved you were not a robot.

In a paper just published in Behavior Research Methods, my colleagues and I used that same task to bring religious ideas to people's minds. Then we checked whether it actually worked.

For about 20 years, psychologists have been asking whether reminding people of God makes them more honest or generous. In his 2013 book Big Gods, Ara Norenzayan argued that belief in a god who watches and punishes helped strangers cooperate once societies grew too large for neighbors to monitor each other. Dominic Johnson had been making a related case since 2004, with more weight on the fear of punishment than on being watched, a point he later expanded in his book God Is Watching You. If either version is right, even a short reminder of God should change behavior in the lab.

The problem is the reminder itself. In implicit priming, participants unscramble sentences containing words like “divine” or “spirit,” in the hope that religious thoughts become active without anyone noticing. These primes are often too weak to demonstrate activation. In explicit priming, participants write a few sentences about God. This works, but many participants can guess what the study is about, and some then behave the way they think a good person should.

The findings have been messy as a result. A 2016 meta-analysis by Azim Shariff and his colleagues concluded that religious priming increases prosocial behavior. But when Michiel van Elk and his colleagues reanalyzed the same data in 2015, two different bias-correction methods yielded different answers: One suggested the entire effect could be explained by publication bias; the other suggested a real effect remained. Their conclusion was that meta-analysis alone cannot settle the question, and that only large, preregistered studies can. A 2024 meta-analysis by Shariff's research group added another twist: The association between religious belief and prosocial behavior appears mostly in what people say about themselves, and much less in what they do.

And almost none of these primes had ever been tested to see whether they really make people think about religion. We assumed they did.

Fırat Şeker, a former master's student of mine who is now pursuing his Ph.D. at UMass Amherst, and Ensar Acem, one of my current Ph.D. students and the manager of our MINT Lab at Kadir Has University in Istanbul, co-led a project to change this.

The idea was to hide the prime inside something people see every day. We built two versions.

In the grid version, participants saw a photo of an open book divided into 16 squares. A short phrase sat in one corner: “God sees,” “God punishes,” “God rewards,” or “God forgives.” The control group saw “He runs” in the same spot. Everyone was told to select the squares with no readable text, just as in an ordinary CAPTCHA.

In the keyword version, participants saw a picture of a Bible and had to pick the word that best described it. The right answer was “sacred,” hidden among options like “train,” “bed,” and “pencil.” The control group saw a photo of a table and had to pick “table” in the same way.

Then came the test. In a preregistered study of 2,770 American Christians, all participants completed a word-completion task. Participants saw fragments such as “f a i _ _” and filled in the blank, which could become “faith” or “faint.” Count the religious words people produce, and you have a behavioral measure of how easily religious thoughts come to mind. After that, participants played a standard dictator game, deciding how much of a small sum to share with a stranger. At the end, we asked them what they thought the study was about.

The explicit prime produced the strongest effect, as expected. But 11 percent of those participants correctly guessed the study's purpose.

The keyword version worked. When people had to find the word “sacred” under a picture of a Bible, they later produced more religious words than the control group did, and the same was true for the versions that pointed to a rewarding or a forgiving God. The version that pointed to a punishing God did not raise religious thoughts in general, but it did raise thoughts about sin and punishment specifically. Only 6 percent of these participants guessed what the study was about. The grid version did not work at all. We told people to select the squares without text, so they barely processed the sentence. A prime can be subtle, but it still needs a few seconds of attention.

Generosity did not change under any prime, including the explicit one. The experimental record here is mixed. In 2018, Joseph Billingsley and his colleagues found that an explicit prime increased giving in a dictator game while an implicit prime did not, and Cristina Gomes and Michael McCullough had found no effect of implicit priming on the same game in 2015. The meta-analytic picture depends on how one corrects for publication bias, as van Elk and his colleagues showed. So a null result is not out of line with what others have found. There is also a design reason. Norenzayan’s point in Big Gods was that religion works when it is in the situation, at the moment a person decides. In our study, the word-completion task came between the prime and the game, so by the time people chose how much to give, the reminder may already have faded. But when a religious prime fails to affect behavior in future studies, researchers can now rule out the most boring explanation: that the prime never reached anyone in the first place.

There is now a tested, low-suspicion method for activating religious thoughts in online studies. It has separate primes for punishing, rewarding, and forgiving images of God. That separation matters. Researchers disagree about whether it is the feeling of being watched or the fear of punishment that makes religious people behave better, and until now there was no clean way to pull the two apart. The materials and data are freely available on OSF.

Almost 10 years ago, Hasan G. Bahçekapili and I argued in Religion, Brain and Behavior that the question “Is religion necessary for morality?” has an easy answer: no, since plenty of people are moral without any religious belief. The harder question, and the one that remains unsolved, is how religion transforms morality once it enters the picture, in our evolutionary past, in history, and in the life of a single person. One reason it stayed unsolved is that we could not trust our own manipulations. Some questions that were put aside as unanswerable may only have been waiting for better tools. The same trick should also work outside religion, for anything that fits in the corner of a picture.

Everyone has heard of the replication crisis in psychology. Its sibling, the validity crisis, gets much less attention. In 2021, David Chester and Emily Lasko reviewed the experimental manipulations used in social psychology and found that most had never been tested to see whether they changed what they were supposed to change. A result can replicate perfectly and still be about nothing in particular.

Validation studies are not glamorous and rarely make the news. But before we ask whether God makes people good, we need to be sure that we have actually made them think about God. The field needs many more studies like this one, and far fewer assumptions.

Bahçekapili, H. G., & Yilmaz, O. (2017). Is religion necessary for morality? Religion, Brain & Behavior, 7(4), 279–281. https://doi.org/10.1080/2153599X.2016.1249924

Billingsley, J., Gomes, C. M., & McCullough, M. E. (2018). Implicit and explicit influences of religious cognition on Dictator Game transfers. Royal Society Open Science, 5(8), 170238. https://doi.org/10.1098/rsos.170238

Chester, D. S., & Lasko, E. N. (2021). Construct validation of experimental manipulations in social psychology: Current practices and recommendations for the future. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 16(2), 377–395. https://doi.org/10.1177/1745691620950684

Johnson, D., & Krüger, O. (2004). The good of wrath: Supernatural punishment and the evolution of cooperation. Political Theology, 5(2), 159–176. https://doi.org/10.1558/poth.2004.5.2.159

Johnson, D. (2015). God Is Watching You: How the Fear of God Makes Us Human. Oxford University Press.

Gomes, C. M., & McCullough, M. E. (2015). The effects of implicit religious primes on dictator game allocations: A preregistered replication experiment. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 144(6), e94–e104. https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0000027

Kelly, J. M., Kramer, S. R., & Shariff, A. F. (2024). Religiosity predicts prosociality, especially when measured by self-report: A meta-analysis of nearly 60 years of research. Psychological Bulletin, 150(3), 284–318. https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000413

Norenzayan, A. (2013). Big Gods: How Religion Transformed Cooperation and Conflict. Princeton University Press.

Shariff, A. F., Willard, A. K., Andersen, T., & Norenzayan, A. (2016). Religious priming: A meta-analysis with a focus on prosociality. Personality and Social Psychology Review, 20(1), 27–48. https://doi.org/10.1177/1088868314568811

Şeker, F., Acem, E., Vurgun, R., Dogruyol, B., Isler, O., & Yilmaz, O. (2026). Divine verification: Introducing a CAPTCHA-based religious priming technique. Behavior Research Methods, 58, 316. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-026-03147-1

van Elk, M., Matzke, D., Gronau, Q. F., Guan, M., Vandekerckhove, J., & Wagenmakers, E.-J. (2015). Meta-analyses are no substitute for registered replications: A skeptical perspective on religious priming. Frontiers in Psychology, 6, Article 1365. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2015.01365

Yilmaz, O., & Bahçekapili, H. G. (2015). Without God, everything is permitted? The reciprocal influence of religious and meta-ethical beliefs. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 58, 95–100. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jesp.2015.01.003

#4755. I finally got a USB-C charging e-bike, and it costs 75% less than Rivian’s bike

I’ve been waiting years for electric bikes to finally embrace USB-C charging. We’ve already standardized much of our lives around the convenient little connector, from phones and laptops to tablets and countless other gadgets. But for some reason, electric bikes have largely missed the memo. Now, though, I’m finally riding an e-bike that charges with USB-C, and the best part is that it doesn’t cost an arm and a leg.

Meet the ENGWE Zip, a quirky little folding electric bike that costs just €999 and has quickly become one of my favorite examples of how a small feature can make a big difference.

When it debuted earlier this year, it became only the third production e-bike I’ve seen that could charge via USB-C, allowing it to use the same charger that is likely already shared by your phone and laptop.

USB-C charging on electric bikes isn’t entirely new, but it’s surprisingly rare. Ampler was one of the first companies to introduce it barely a year ago, though its bikes are sadly no longer in production after the company’s bankruptcy. More recently, Rivian’s ALSO electric bike arrived with USB-C charging, but that bike costs around $4,500 – at least if you want the model that’s slowly starting to ship.

The ENGWE Zip, on the other hand, costs roughly a quarter as much as its only USB-charging competition. At €999, it’s priced at a relatively affordable US$1,100. That’s a quarter of the cost of the only other USB-C charging e-bike on the market.

Of course, it’s not nearly as technologically advanced as Rivian’s ALSO e-bike. But hey, it’s at least shipping.

And while the Zip is a fun little 16″ wheel folding electric bike in its own right, with a compact design that makes it easy to store and transport, it’s the charging setup that has me particularly excited.

Instead of keeping track of yet another proprietary charging brick, I can simply grab the USB-C charger from my laptop and plug it into the bike. There’s one in my living room by the couch. There’s one by my bed. There’s one in all of my friends’ places. There’s a USB-C charger everywhere.

If I’m traveling around, that means one less charger to pack. If I’m visiting someone, there’s a decent chance they already have a compatible charger sitting around.

Heck, I can even use a basic USB-C phone charger in a pinch. Sure, charging a relatively large e-bike battery at 20W isn’t going to be particularly quick, but the fact that I can do it at all is incredibly convenient.

Plus, the bike has one more trick. The battery also outputs USB-C, so I can charge my laptop or other devices from it as well. I can even charge two devices simultaneously, thanks to the dual USB-C ports.

The battery is housed in a roll-top bag that is locked into the headset of the bike but can be quickly unlocked for charging off the bike. And since it’s a keyed lock, no one can steal the battery even when the bag is left on the bike.

I typically charge the battery still mounted on the bike, though occasionally when I want to use a friend’s USB-C charger, I’ll just pop the bag off and bring it right up to wherever the closest USB-C charger is located.

It may not be the fastest charge, but it’s pretty darn convenient. And with a 360Wh battery, a powerful 100W laptop charger will still get it pretty much full in 4 hours, or for a more typical 50% recharge, roughly two hours.

And that’s really the beauty of USB-C charging. It’s not necessarily about charging faster. It’s about having options. It’s about not being stuck if the very specific charger that only works on your e-bike doesn’t happen to be around exactly where you are.

Of course, there’s a technical reason we haven’t seen USB-C charging spread across the e-bike industry quite as quickly as it has with smaller electronics. Most e-bike batteries operate at 36V or 48V nominal, meaning their charging voltages are higher than the 20V typically supplied by common USB-C laptop chargers. That requires additional voltage conversion and charging circuitry inside the bike or battery.

But clearly, it can be done. And if ENGWE can offer it on a €999 electric bike, there’s a pretty compelling argument that more manufacturers should be taking a serious look at the technology. In this case, it’s all housed inside the battery, meaning it could be directly incorporated into any e-bike whose manufacturer is brave enough to spec it.

USB-C charging aside, there's a very good reason that just about every folding e-bike on the market has put thick plates on the folding connection of the frame. It's because the frame breaks if they're not there. Just like this one is going to.

I’m not suggesting that every e-bike needs to abandon its dedicated charger tomorrow. For larger batteries, high-powered chargers still make plenty of sense, especially when you want to get back on the road quickly.

But having USB-C as an additional charging option? That’s something I’d love to see become standard.

For years, we’ve seen how electric bikes are becoming more convenient, more practical, and better integrated into our everyday lives. Yet when it comes to charging, we’re still carrying around a collection of more or less proprietary chargers.

Now I’m riding a barely $1k electric bike that can charge from the same power brick as my laptop. And frankly, I think it’s about time the rest of the e-bike industry caught up!

FTC: We use income earning auto affiliate links. More.

Micah Toll is a personal electric vehicle enthusiast, battery nerd, and author of the Amazon #1 bestselling books DIY Lithium Batteries, DIY Solar Power, The Ultimate DIY Ebike Guide and The Electric Bike Manifesto.

The e-bikes that make up Micah’s current daily drivers are the $999 Lectric XP 2.0, the $1,095 Ride1Up Roadster V2, the $1,199 Rad Power Bikes RadMission, and the $3,299 Priority Current. But it’s a pretty evolving list these days.

#4753. Narrative and Illness: The Autobiographical Stories We Tell Matter

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Humans love stories. From oral storytelling to novels to movies and television—we make sense of our world through narrative. Through stories, we seek to understand ourselves and be understood by others. Stories are especially important in identity construction. That is, we define ourselves in large part by the narrative we tell about who we are. As identity is profoundly changed by illness, how do we work with our narrative to reflect this shift?

For most people, illness is a “biographical disruption.” It’s an unexpected and often devastating event that blows up life as we’ve known it. We become acquainted with pain, fear, loneliness, and limitations. The people we were before illness could count on our bodies to work. The people we were before illness understood suffering as an abstract concept rather than as a lived experience. The people we were before illness had freedom in moving through the world that we took entirely for granted.

When illness strikes, we experience deep grief. We mourn for the things we have lost, especially our pre-illness identity. The grief is necessary, as we can never be who we once were. As we go through the grief process, we have to make a narrative decision: Is illness the end of our story, or is there a way our story can continue?

In their article “Volition as Narrative: Understanding Motivation in Chronic Illness,” Helfrich, Kielhofner, & Mattingly (1994) describe two people whose lives have been interrupted by serious illness. One individual continues to fight for his lifelong dream of being a reporter. He’s had to reconceptualize what this will look like. While he may never write for a prestigious national publication, he finds ways to continue reporting for smaller outlets, pivoting as needed. He says, “[P]eople who don’t get sick make [long-term] plans. Every plan that I’ve made has eventually been defeated and I’ve had to shift to another subplan.” But he keeps shifting, as many times as he needs to. He keeps writing more chapters of his life story.

The other case study in the article describes a woman who has not been able to make a meaningful life for herself post-illness. She says, “I feel like I got cheated out of my life.” In contrast to the first case study, her story ended with illness. No further chapters were written.

One important narrative concept is “character.” How often do we read or watch a story and remark on the characters presented? While the events that occur in a story are certainly important, the intersection of plot with character is what makes stories so meaningful. In the article discussed above, for example, the reporter is a richly developed character. He is smart, determined, and resourceful. He is resilient. His sense of himself as a character with these traits enables him to meet the plot twist in his story with the strengths he believes himself to possess.

If I were working with the woman in the article, I’d want to get a sense of who she imagines herself to be as a character in her own life story. I’m guessing she may never have thought about herself in this way. I would ask her to tell me what she was like as a kid: What did she enjoy playing? Who did she enjoy playing with? I would ask her to tell me what she wanted for herself prior to illness and what she hopes for herself now. I would ask her to tell me what traits she values in herself and in others. I would ask her to flesh out for me who she is as a character in her own story. Undoubtedly, we would discover character traits we could build upon, strengths that might guide her as she imagines continuing her narration post-illness.

Another important narrative concept is “other characters.” Stories typically involve characters interacting with other characters. In the article, the reporter mentions the support his mother gave him. By contrast, the woman speaks of an interaction with a doctor in which he told her that her illness would prevent her from ever finishing college. As in novels and films, other people are tremendously important in our life stories. In our own stories, who are the characters that support us, that help us along the way? Who are the characters who cut us down and make our lives feel smaller and harder? How can we invite in supportive characters while minimizing the damage done by non-supportive characters?

“Narratives are created between people” (Ellis-Hill, Payne, & Ward, 2008). A novel has readers. A movie has watchers. A story has listeners. We create stories because we want to be seen and understood. We listen to stories because we want to see and understand. What is the story you want to tell about your life? Who do you want to listen?

If you’ve never thought about your life story, or if your life story needs a rewrite, therapy is a great place to do this work. Like an editor, therapists can often see elements of a story that the writer can’t. We can help you identify threads of meaning that run through your story (themes), and we can help you view your story in different ways (perspectives). Most importantly, we can help you with the chapter you are writing right now, in the present. What do you want this chapter to look like? Who can you imagine yourself to be in these unchosen circumstances? It’s your story: What are you going to write?

Ellis-Hill, C., Payne, S., & Ward, C. (2008). Using stroke to explore the life thread model: an alternative approach to understanding rehabilitation following an acquired disability. Disability and Rehabilitation, 30(2), 150–159.

Helfrich, C., Kielhofner, G., & Mattingly, C. (1994). Volition as narrative: Understanding motivation in chronic illness. American Journal of Occupational Therapy, 48(4), 311–317.

#4752. Tesla Cybercab’s autonomy agreement is insane: $299/mo or it doesn’t move

Tesla has posted the agreement that comes with its $29,990 Cybercab, and it’s even worse than the order page suggested. The two-seater can’t move without a $299 monthly “Autonomy Subscription” that Tesla can reprice with a month’s notice, suspend for a week, or cut off entirely.

And Tesla wants consumers to sign it while still refusing to give unsupervised self-driving to the Model Y owners it has been selling “Full Self-Driving” to for nearly a decade.

The “Cybercab Autonomy Subscription Agreement” (version 20261112) went up on Tesla’s configurator late Friday, hours after the company started inviting select customers to order the Cybercab for personal use at $29,990 plus a mandatory $299 per month.

The key line is short: “Your Cybercab will not operate without an active Autonomy Subscription.” There’s no steering wheel and no pedals, so that isn’t a figure of speech. Stop paying and you have a $30,000 object in your garage.

That personal-use clause kills the whole pitch. For years, Musk told people they’d buy a Tesla, add it to the fleet, and make money while they sleep. The first Tesla sold to consumers for unsupervised operation is contractually barred from doing exactly that.

Then there’s the geofence. Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas are already smaller in practice than advertised: when we tested them, real coverage was between 59% and 78% of the advertised maps, and parts of the Houston map have been called “fake” by the person tracking it. Now Tesla reserves the right to shrink that area after you’ve paid for the car.

Mark Valorian, who went through the terms on X, summed it up as “an endless variable-rate lease with a ridiculous down payment.” That’s about right.

Over five years, the car plus 59 paid months of subscription comes to $47,631 before insurance, registration, charging, and taxes, all of which are on the owner.

This is the part that should make every Tesla owner angry.

Tesla has spent the last year telling everyone that its Model Y is just as much a robotaxi as the Cybercab. Ahead of the Robotaxi launch in Austin, Musk said the cars were “the Model Ys we make currently, there’s no change to it.” On Tesla’s Q3 2026 earnings call last month, AI chief Ashok Elluswamy said Cybercabs and Model Y robotaxis already run the same software, and that customer cars might join the network around Q2 2027. The Cybercab launches on the same AI4 computer found in the current Model Y.

So the hardware is the same, the software is the same, and unsupervised Model Ys are already operating in the exact geofences where Cybercab owners will be allowed to ride.

Yet the people who paid for it get nothing. Tesla started selling “Full Self-Driving Capability” in 2016 on the promise that every car it built had the hardware for it. Owners paid up to $15,000 for the package. In February, Tesla stopped selling it outright and moved to a $99 per month subscription, which still requires you to supervise the car at all times.

Tesla’s answer to all those owners is a new car. One with two seats, no controls, a geofence it can move whenever it wants, and a subscription that costs three times as much as FSD.

I’ll say it plainly: this car is for suckers who want to give their money to Elon Musk.

You don’t own a Cybercab in any meaningful sense. You pay $30,000 for the right to keep paying Tesla $299 a month, at a price Tesla can raise, in an area Tesla can shrink, under rules Tesla enforces, with a camera pointed at you the whole time.

There are three possible reasons Tesla isn't allowing model Y owners to use FSD in the allowed zones:

1: the robotaxis are in fact different from the model Ys being sold

2: Tesla doesn't have enough "remote operators" to cover all of those supposedly self-driving cars if users join the network

3: Tesla isn't willing to accept liability when FSD kills someone.

And the Model Y part is what gives the game away. If Tesla truly believed its unsupervised system was ready for customers, the obvious move would be to turn it on for the Model Y owners in Austin who already paid for it. It’s the same computer and the same software in the same geofence. But that would mean honoring a promise made in 2016, on cars already sold, with no new revenue attached.

A new vehicle wipes that slate clean. No legacy FSD buyers, no HW3 baggage, just a fresh customer locked into a $299 monthly fee from day one. What Tesla built is a subscription with a $30,000 entry fee attached to it.

So what happens the first time Tesla emails Cybercab owners a month’s notice that the price is going to $399?

#4751. Potatoes grown in moon dirt are as nutritious as Earth potatoes

🛍️ Live: The best Black Friday deals on stuff you actually want 🛍️

Published Nov 19, 2026 5:00 AM EST

Astronauts living in the first permanent lunar base may see a sizable number of spuds on their dinner plates. In a study published today in the journal npj Microgravity, botanists at Oregon State University (OSU) proved it’s possible to grow healthy, edible potatoes in simulated moon soil with the help of everyday worms. Importantly, the team also identified the proper proportions of lunar regolith and compost needed to produce potato yields similar to those grown on Earth.

“We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter,” Aymeric Goyer, an OSU botanist and study co-author, said in a statement. “That’s an important step toward developing reliable food production systems that could support long-term human exploration of the Moon.”

Even in a controlled habitat, life on the moon will be physically demanding for astronauts. They’ll require carefully maintained, nutritious diets to keep them healthy, but it’s not as simple as sending them off packed with calorically dense prepackaged meals. Cargo room on spacecraft is limited and costly, and the desolate lunar surface isn’t exactly hospitable to agriculture. In addition to constant bombardment by cosmic and solar radiation, temperatures can swing anywhere between 250 degrees and -410 degrees Fahrenheit.

Indoor horticulture will also be challenging. Lunar regolith is an annoyingly powdery substance composed of sharp-edged, miniscule particles created over billions of years of asteroid impacts, but little else. With essentially no organic material at all, the dust alone isn’t capable of supporting plant life.

While it is easy enough to combine that lunar regolith with agricultural additives, researchers weren’t sure if these could overcome moon soil’s heavy metals and irradiation. To test it, Goyer and his colleagues first obtained simulated lunar regolith made to resemble the samples collected during the Apollo missions. Regolith composition varies by region on the moon, so they selected five different types based on darker lunar mare dust and the lighter lunar highland soil. They then mixed the mock moon dust with vermicompost, the nutrient-rich soil created when worms break down organic materials. Next, they planted potatoes in various ratios of regolith and vermicompost, and monitored their growth. As a control, the team even planted potatoes in soil taken from Hermiston, Oregon, an area famous for some of the world’s highest spud yields.

The team found that composite soil with only 30 percent vermicompost was enough to produce potato crops comparable to those farmed on Earth. Their findings suggest the supplemental organics bind to the regolith’s heavy metals, which shield the plants and minimize any damage to their roots.

“We believe the compost helps balance some of the toxicity we see in lunar regolith,” added OSU botanist and study co-author David Handy.

But bushels of moon potatoes only go so far if they lack any real nutritional value. Even here, the lunar simulations offered promising results, particularly when it came to glycoalkaloids. The naturally forming potato toxins can cause green skin discoloration, but analysis indicated no statistically relevant rise in glycoalkaloids for the lunar crops.

With the potato viability debate settled, Goyer’s team will next compare 10 specific spud varieties grown in simulated lunar regolith to determine the most nutritious and resilient options for NASA astronomers.

#4750. 6 to 8 Cups of Tea Daily May Reduce Heart Disease Risk by 11%

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

People who regularly drink tea may have an 11% lower overall risk of vascular disease, which includes conditions such as stroke, heart disease, and peripheral artery disease. This is according to a study published on October 21 in the Journal of Internal Medicine.

Both black tea and green tea may offer heart health benefits. However, the study shows an association rather than proving that drinking tea prevents cardiovascular disease.

The lowest overall vascular risk was seen among tea drinkers who were also physically active and didn’t smoke.

The study followed 485,934 people ages 30–79 from the China Kadoorie Biobank for an average of 9 years.

The researchers found that regular tea drinkers had an 11% lower overall risk of vascular disease compared with those who did not regularly drink tea. They also observed a 37% lower risk of ischemic stroke and a 17% lower risk of heart attack.

There was no clear link for hemorrhagic stroke or pulmonary heart disease.

Among people who drank tea at least weekly, the lowest estimated risk was seen in those consuming approximately 6–8 cups per day. However, the findings do not establish this as a recommended daily intake.

Amit Blumfield, MD, a cardiologist with Manhattan Cardiology in NYC who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that it is important to remember this is observational data.

Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) examining the effects of drinking black and green tea on lipids and blood pressure showed only modest, non-significant benefits.

The study also had limitations, including self-reported tea consumption and the possibility that other dietary and lifestyle factors influenced the results.

“Overall, tea seems to, maybe, have some cardiovascular benefits without a significant risk, so I favor tea consumption,” he said.

Michelle Routhenstein, a preventive cardiology dietitian at Entirely Nourished who was not involved in the research, emphasized that the findings do not establish a cause-and-effect relationship between drinking tea and a lower risk of vascular disease.

“Tea can be a helpful addition to a heart-healthy lifestyle, but it is not a substitute for addressing individual cardiovascular risk factors,” she said.

The researchers also found that drinking “burning hot” tea increased the risk of vascular disease by 16%, consistent with previous research raising concerns about the consumption of very hot beverages.

“I recommend enjoying your tea’s potential benefits by letting it cool to a comfortable sipping temperature before you drink it,” said Routhenstein.

The study examined black, green, Oolong, and other tea types.

The researchers found that black tea showed a more consistent association with a lower risk of vascular disease, which is contrary to some earlier research. However, they noted that these results don’t establish black tea as superior to green tea, and they don’t mean you should switch tea types.

“Both black and green tea are great choices for your heart health, and neither is definitively better than the other,” said Routhenstein.

“I recommend choosing whichever you enjoy and consuming it consistently, ideally without much added sugar,” Routhenstein noted.

Blumfield also noted that adding sugar or non-sugar sweeteners may change the potential health effects of drinking tea, so the findings should not automatically be extended to sweetened tea beverages.

Some older research suggests there may be additional health benefits to drinking both black and green tea. These benefits may include:

Routhenstein said that tea may also support focus and alertness, improve hydration status, and potentially play a role in metabolic health.

“Enjoying tea can be a simple way to incorporate beneficial plant compounds into your day,” she added.

While drinking tea has been considered a health-promoting habit since ancient times, more research is needed to confirm its various health benefits.

#4749. Beyond 'Forgive and Forget': 5 Practical Relationship Habits

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

In an era dominated by relationship burnout and hyper-individualism, many couples find themselves trapped in endless cycles of friction and emotional distance. Breaking free requires adopting habits that run counter to modern culture. Here are some counterintuitive relationship habits you could consider adopting or adapting to fit the unique rhythm and idiosyncrasies of your (current or future) intimate relationship.

Life is a process of displacement. When you are born, you immediately become #1. As long as you are single, you remain #1—it’s still about you and your freedom.

When you get married, you become #2. You have to learn to put your spouse first (without compromising your deeply held values—that’s why choosing the right person is the most important decision you’ll ever make) if you want the marriage to work.

When you have a child, you become #3. By the time you become a grandparent, you’re lucky if you’re still in the Top 10.

While it sounds like you become weaker, it’s the opposite: You become stronger. While it sounds like you become a follower, it’s, again, the opposite: This is true leadership. The front-stage star is not a leader, but a showman—not the director, but an actor.

The true leader is the one you don’t see, the back-stage architect whose undying devotion enables the unfolding drama, which involves many, to captivate and enthrall, night after night.

Twenty-five years ago, I was wrestling with my inner demons about commitment and went on a walk along the Potomac River outside of Washington, DC, with a close family friend who had been married to his wife for more than 40 years.

“How have you managed being married for so long?” I asked him.

Robert looked at the turbulent rapids and thought for a while. Then he said, “The best advice I ever received was from my aunt, while I was fixing my tuxedo just before Charlene and I were married.”

“She said, ‘Robert, always remember this: Whatever Charlene does, just give. No matter what happens, always give. And the two of you will be fine.’”

I’ll pass on Robert’s aunt’s sage advice: Just give. No matter what. It’s your only power. You control how, when, and what to give.

What you receive, on the other hand, is completely out of your control. Yet the more and better you give, the more love will also come in your direction.

In other words, let things go. There are two things you do in life: You choose how you want to live, and you live with what you choose.

You chose a long-term commitment to this person, which means letting lots of things (but not everything) go. Consider that the opposite of forgiveness is resentment. A word derived from the Latin roots re (again) and sentire (to feel), resentment is to feel anger again and again until you become paralyzed.

Forgiveness is a better option: while resentment paralyzes, forgiveness liberates.

As children, we’re often told by adults—generally with good intentions—to “forgive and forget.” To forget, however, may not be the best idea.

If you fall into a ditch, the last thing you want to do is forget the location of the ditch. Such a strategy may result in your falling in again.

A better way to approach forgiveness is to acknowledge what the other person did, file it away, give for the other person to yourself, and then let it go. This approach need not include your tolerating the same behavior again.

Forgiveness, in fact, does not necessarily lead to a continued relationship. In many cases, forgiveness enables you to detach yourself from the relationship, not only physically but also emotionally and psychologically.

Importantly, while trust binds, forgiveness releases. While forgiveness is needed for personal development, trust is needed for relational development.

Trust is not necessarily an evolutionary adaptive behavior, as it can lead to more harmful behavior from the other person. A man can apologize to his wife for an affair, for example, regain her trust, and then continue to cheat on her afterward.

While trusting a specific person whom you feel has harmed you is not necessary for your evolution as a human being, forgiving them is. Forgiveness is one of your most critical attributes because until you let go of your suffering, you don’t let it recede from the present and into the past.

Until you forgive and then learn to love any person in your life, you remain trapped in a drama with them. You remain on their stage, entangled in an invisible thread that binds you to them.

You may be acting out the drama with the surrogates you bring into your life to replace them, but you are still cast in the role. This is how love liberates, how love sets you free.

The more you are able to take this cognitive step toward understanding and respecting innate differences that will always be beyond your control, the more inner peace and happiness you will invite into your life.

If you are like most of us, you probably have not yet made this transformative decision. You have likely spent most of your life preoccupied with the comings and goings and machinations and preferences of the other characters in your story—including and especially your partner—instead of seeing them as they are: as other human beings who enter and exit your stage throughout your life.

How can you accept yourself and others as you and they are while also retaining your optimism about what you and they can become?

#4745. The Benefits of Having an Older Sibling During Adolescence

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Adolescence is an important time when young people seek independence from their parents, focusing on friends and romantic partners and figuring out who they want to be. As teens navigate these important developmental tasks, they will learn and grow with the help of others. For adolescents with an older sibling, that sibling can be an important, trusted family resource who helps guide them during this developmental period.

While siblings do spend less time together during adolescence, their relationship remains important and influential for youths' social, emotional, and cognitive development. In fact, adolescents report sharing and discussing personal information and thoughts with their siblings daily. Although older siblings are not always a positive influence, they can play a beneficial role in the lives of younger siblings during adolescence.

In the United States, most siblings are about two years apart in age, creating likely similarities in their life experiences. These similarities, along with siblings’ shared family history and special understanding of one another, can make an older sibling an ideal resource during adolescence. A sibling can also provide an alternative source of support for youth who may not feel comfortable talking to their parents or need a different perspective.

Teens may also seek out their older siblings as relatable confidants, perhaps using them as a sounding board before approaching their parents or other adults. Adolescents may enjoy the back-and-forth conversation with their sibling more than top-down pressure from parents. Reflecting this trust, research shows that adolescent siblings frequently talk about their daily activities, media use, nonfamilial relationships, academics, and future plans.

During adolescence, sibling support is often mutual, especially when navigating family matters. However, older siblings generally have more influence on younger siblings than vice versa, often adopting a teacher or mentor role even if they are only a few years older. Younger siblings often admire and look up to their older siblings. This status typically happens because of birth order and age: Older siblings are likely to face social situations with peers and romantic partners, encounter academic challenges and classes, and make decisions about future plans before their younger siblings.

Does it matter if an adolescent has an older brother or sister? The findings are mixed, with some studies showing no effect. Other studies show that younger siblings receive more guidance and support from same-sex rather than opposite-sex older siblings. This is thought to happen because same-sex siblings share greater similarities and relate to each other more easily. Additionally, older sisters are often close confidants and mentors for younger sisters and provide more advice than older brothers do. For example, one study found that older sisters give younger sisters specific instructions and information about dating and romantic relationships.

Older siblings can influence adolescent younger siblings in several ways, including by guiding them through direct instruction and encouragement or by providing information and advice. Another way older siblings influence younger siblings is by serving as role models. By watching their older siblings’ activities, choices, and subsequent consequences, younger siblings learn from them.

Older brothers and sisters are invaluable guides promoting positive development for their less experienced younger siblings in a variety of areas, including dating and peer relationships, body image, and prosocial skills like empathy. One study showed that older siblings shape adolescents’ social skills and their athletic and artistic interests, particularly when older siblings excelled in those areas. Other work found that how much adolescents discussed extracurricular activities, media, and academics with their older siblings was linked to their success in friendships, sports, and school.

Parents can encourage strong, loving sibling relationships in which older siblings serve as positive role models and resources for younger siblings during adolescence through the following suggestions:

Killoren, S. E., & Roach, A. L. (2014). Sibling conversations about dating and sexuality: Sisters as confidants, sources of support, and mentors. Family Relations, 63(2), 232–243. https://doi.org/10.1111/fare.12057

Tucker, C. J., & Winzeler, A. (2007). Adolescent siblings’ daily discussions: Connections to perceived academic, athletic, and peer competency. Journal of Research on Adolescence, 17(1), 145–152. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1532-7795.2007.00515.x

Whiteman, S. D., & Christiansen, A. (2008). Processes of sibling influence in adolescence: Individual and family correlates. Family Relations, 57(1), 24–34. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1741-3729.2007.00480.x

We all know the type: grizzled stubble, wraparound PitVipers, a MAGA hat quietly retired after last week’s deep-blue shellacking, and a pristine, polished pickup parked in the driveway that they “need for towing.” With Stellantis’ new patent for an AI-powered electric tow dolly that turns just about ANY vehicle into a capable tow rig, however, those might need a new to find a new excuse to keep that gas-guzzler.

Originally filed in 2023, Stellantis received US Patent No. 12,779,916 for its electric tow dolly on 03NOV2026. The patent covers a machine that’s designed to shoulder the trailer’s hitch load with its own ball hitch or fifth-wheel plate, using an on-board electric motor and battery to get the trailer going while its regenerative braking system and AI-backed steering and traction control system keeps everything pointed in the right direction.

In other words, the dolly takes on many of the jobs that traditionally require a big tow vehicle: providing the pulling power, managing the trailer’s weight and controlling its braking and traction. The vehicle up front doesn’t necessarily need a massive motor, heavy-duty suspension or oversized brakes. With a system like this, you could argue that the “tow vehicle” isn’t really a tow vehicle at all. It’s more of a “lead vehicle,” since the dolly is the one doing the towing … and it can follow just about anything – including the diminutive (and supremely affordable) Fiat 500e, which is also made by Stellantis.

To be clear, this isn’t just Uncle Jojo making fun of the commuter conveys – Stellantis’ patent describes the dolly as being equipped with an autonomous control system using cameras, sensors, a controller, and an advanced, four wheel steer-by-wire system. It also specifically discusses how the dolly’s independently powered acceleration, braking and steering, and sway controls essentially remove the need to own a truck in the first place.

The dolly system’s truck bed sides and small size allow users to experience the functionality and utility of a truck only when they need it, allowing them to own a smaller, cheaper, and more fuel efficient vehicle that suits daily use needs.

There are some pretty obvious practical questions still to answer, of course, including how much battery capacity the dolly would need, how much weight it could handle and how it would perform on long grades or in emergency braking situations. And, to be clear, a patent isn’t a product announcement or proof that Stellantis plans to put one of these things on sale – heck, if I were Stellantis’ CEO, I’d patent this thing just to prevent anyone else from building one so I could keep selling ancient, low-tech, high-margin Ram Trucks – but it’s a neat idea.

Okay, I like this idea and appreciate the problem it is trying to solve, but it has the same challenge as any electric-tow situation, which is the charging logistics. Even if you find a pull-through charger (very rare), if you are using an EV, you still need to charge two "vehicles," so you have to charge your car, then pull up and charge the dolly afterwards. Even if you are using a gas car, charging the dolly will be logistically challenging. Of course, that's a problem with an easy solution (more pull-through chargers), but also one that doesn't seem to be on any charging network's radar.

I think it’s neat, anyway. What do you guys think? Are you ready to trade in your big-battery Chevy Silverado EV or Volvo VNR 800 on a new Topolino, or are you going to keep driving inefficient 99% of the time? Let us know, in the comments.

Published Nov 19, 2026 7:53 AM EST

Becky the basset hound is giving new meaning to the term “man’s best friend.” On November 12, she walked to the Whiteface Lodge, a ski resort in Lake Placid, New York. The hotel staff immediately recognized the dog, but not because of her sparkling personality or floppy ears. Becky’s owner has dementia, and the unnamed man has disappeared before.

The team at Whiteface called the New York State Police (NYSP), who contacted the Department of Conservation (DEC) Forest Rangers for assistance with the search. Four NYSP officers and 14 Rangers used drones and another dog (a bloodhound) to search for the missing person. According to Charlie Foutch, the lead Ranger on the search, it was about 25 to 30 degrees Fahrenheit overnight.

At 10 a.m. the next morning, a hunter who was searching just ahead of the group heard someone fall and scream. He found the missing man off to the side of a trail in a draining area with open woods. Ranger Sabo arrived on the scene shortly after. The 69-year-old man was not wearing gloves or shoes, and was suffering from some frostbite on his feet and hands. He was still alert and talking.

“We’re always looking for live people. That’s our goal is to find a live person,” said Fouch. “And a lot of people are really tough. This gentleman didn’t have shoes on when we found him in the morning or mittens or gloves, so he had been out there for some period of time at night. And he still did okay. Sometimes if you keep moving in that situation, you generate enough heat to do okay.”

Due to his injuries and the location off the trail, a hoist was the safest and quickest way to get him to safety. Ranger Martin used a cable to hoist him up to a helicopter, while NYSP Pilot Engle flew them to the hospital.

In addition to this coordination between hunters, the NYSP, and DEC, Fouch said that Becky the basset hound made this happy ending possible.

“I think if the dog had not shown up at Whiteface, that gentleman definitely would have had a different outcome,” said Fouch. “It definitely would have been much harder to find him. He may not have survived the rest of the day and probably not another night. The dog definitely contributed to him being saved so quickly.”

#4741. Why Real Paintings Can Look AI-Generated

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Take a look at the two moonlit scenes below. One was painted in 1839. The other was generated by artificial intelligence (AI) in 2026. Which one would you choose as being the work of a human artist?

Before looking for the answer, consider what guided your choice. The light? The details? Perhaps one looks a little too polished, while the other feels more natural. How confident are you that those qualities tell you who made it?

I find this question interesting because it asks us to examine something we might otherwise take for granted: what human creativity is supposed to look like.

In a preliminary, unpublished study, I asked 202 U.S. adults to judge images drawn from five 19th-century paintings and five AI-generated versions of the same scenes. Each participant saw five images, presented individually in random order, and identified each as human-made, AI-generated, or something they were unsure about.

Among the 920 answers that named a source, participants were correct about 45 percent of the time. For these images, that was below the 50 percent expected from a coin flip.

But the direction of the mistakes was more interesting. Participants labeled the original paintings as AI-generated 51 percent of the time. They gave that label to the actual AI images only 42 percent of the time. The original looked more artificial than its AI counterpart in four of the five pairs.

And the answer to the opening question? Image A is Johan Christian Dahl’s View of Dresden by Moonlight, painted in 1839. Image B is AI-generated. Among definite answers, 69 percent labeled Dahl’s painting AI, compared with 51 percent for the generated version.

This reversal has a parallel in poetry. Brian Porter and Edouard Machery found that nonexpert readers were more likely to attribute AI-generated poems to humans than poems actually written by established poets (2024). Our expectations about human expression can apparently lead us away from the humans.

Why might this happen? Participants’ explanations offered a clue. Nearly a quarter mentioned a polished or “too perfect” appearance as a sign of AI. That seems like a reasonable suspicion until we consider how much effort painters have devoted to achieving precisely those qualities.

Consider the still life below. The original is Image B, painted by Severin Roesen in 1852. Its elaborate arrangement and luminous fruit might fit someone’s idea of what an image generator produces. Yet here those qualities belong to a human painter.

One possible explanation is what psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman called the representativeness heuristic: judging something by how closely it resembles our idea of a category (1974). If our mental picture of AI art is smooth, detailed, and beautifully lit, a painting with those features may seem machine-made. (This is an interpretation of the findings; the study did not experimentally establish that polish caused the mistakes.)

Experience offered little reassurance. Regular users of AI image tools were less likely to answer “not sure,” but showed no detectable accuracy advantage. Being comfortable making a judgment and being correct about it are separate matters.

Of course, five painting pairs cannot tell us how people judge all art. Participants viewed digital reproductions, and each made only five judgments. The results do not establish that expertise is useless or that nobody can detect AI. They do suggest that familiar visual clues can mislead us in this particular setting.

That matters because authorship can change appreciation. In experiments by Lucas Bellaiche and colleagues, artworks received more favorable evaluations when labeled human-created rather than AI-created, even though all the images were generated by AI (2023). The story we attach to an image can become part of what we see in it.

What gives me pause is the possibility that we might dismiss human skill precisely because it looks accomplished. Before treating an image as obviously artificial, I would want to know more about where it came from.

Dahl painted that moonlit scene in 1839. The suspicion that it looks like AI belongs entirely to us.

Porter, B., & Machery, E. (2024). AI-generated poetry is indistinguishable from human-written poetry and is rated more favorably. Scientific Reports, 14, 26133. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-76900-1

Tversky, A., & Kahneman, D. (1974). Judgment under uncertainty: Heuristics and biases. Science, 185(4157), 1124–1131. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.185.4157.1124

Bellaiche, L., Shahi, R., Turpin, M. H., Ragnhildstveit, A., Sprockett, S., Barr, N., Christensen, A., & Seli, P. (2023). Humans versus AI: Whether and why we prefer human-created compared to AI-created artwork. Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications, 8, 42. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41235-023-00499-6

#4739. $20K Nissan NX7 PHEV goes on sale with nearly 200 miles of electric range

Dongfeng Nissan officially opened the early order book on its new NX7 hybrid yesterday, promising up to 320 km (~198 miles) of all-electric range from a 40 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery and a $20,000 price tag.

When the first generation Nissan LEAF bowed with 70-ish miles of range from its 24 kWh li-ion battery pack, it struggled to meet widespread adoption, especially in an SUV-obsessed US market that demands forethought-free trips to Home Depot and bladder-busting range. The company’s latest 2027 Rogue Hybrid is a step in the right direction, using a gas engine to generate electricity for a pair of electric drive motors that deliver a driving experience that’s remarkably similar to a “pure” electric car – but without a plug, it’s still entirely dependent on fossil fuels. The new Dongfeng Nissan NX7, though? That’s a different story.

The plug-in hybrid Dongfeng Nissan NX7 might be called a “long range hybrid” in the same sense that Volvo’s Euro-market XC70 is, in that it’s an EV for the 360-odd days a year that you’re driving less than 200 miles, and an ICE vehicle for the handful of days you drive more. And if you’re one of those people who thinks stopping on road trips is a character flaw, a fully charged and topped off NX7 will take you an astonishing 1,666 km (~1,035 miles) from where you started.

The new NX7 could be an ideal lilypad vehicle for North American drivers who are either too afraid of being caught without a charger or too invested in the outcome of one or more dumb oil wars to confidently make the switch to EV – and, even at twice the 129,900 yuan ($~19,400) asking price, I think it would be a hit.

For that money, NX7 buyers get an absolutely loaded Model Y-sized crossover (they’re within 1/4″ of each other in length), with a 17.3″ central touchscreen, a fully digital instrument cluster, and (on higher-spec models) a positively massive 55″ augmented-reality head-up display powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8295P automotive processor and running on Nissan OS 3.0 with an AI-powered voice assistant developed with iFlytek that, Nissan claims, can recognize natural-language commands, remember user preferences, and even recognize occupants, adjusting vehicle settings accordingly.

On top-shelf models, the NX7 cabins get “AI Zero-Pressure Cloud Blanket” seats that use sensors and air-cushion arrays to dynamically adjust for maximum comfort, and include heating, ventilation, and a 12-point SPA-level massage function. The front seats can be fully reclined to create a bed-like configuration that will be familiar to Cube owners. The NX7 even offers an on-board refrigerator and motion-sickness prevention system that Nissan claims can reduce motion sickness by as much as 83% (which, like, I wouldn’t want to be the one to test that – but seems cool).

Power comes from a 1.5-liter naturally aspirated internal combustion engine making 98 hp that’s paired to a 228 hp electric drive motor and the previously mentioned 40.9 kWh LFP battery. It’s not immediately clear if the NX7 uses a conventional parallel hybrid system like a Prius or a series-hybrid-plus-plug setup, but Dongfeng’s hybrid technology patents describe a pretty versatile arrangement with four possible operating modes: series hybrid, parallel hybrid, direct engine drive and electricity generation – which means the vehicle can theoretically use the ICE motor as a generator, drive the wheels mechanically, or work alongside the electric motor, depending on what the operating conditions call for. Whether any or all four modes make it to production on the NX7 remains to be seen, but it’s an intriguing bit of engineering for a vehicle promising nearly 200 miles of electric driving range.

Why is this article written like it will be available in the US market? It’s made in China and has Chinese software, we’ll never see it

The final production version will be shown to the public for the first time at the Guangzhou Auto Show later this month, but you can let us know what you think of the new NX7 in the comments, today.
